citations.quote: The proposed model-based approach is the result of experience gained from the MASAT1 project, a Moroccan university nanosatellite, and it is based on an architectural framework that allows the system to be described via a set of views.

The combination of Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) and Systems Modeling Language (SysML) emerged as an alternative management and design approach that improves mission reliability by focusing on the engineering aspects of projects.

The aim of using MBSE for a nanosatellite project is to create a model framework or repository that can be used by university teams (with limited resources) wishing to design CubeSat or Nanosatellite projects.
We used No Magic MagicDraw modeler with SysML and Cameo Simulation toolkit plugin.

The functional requirements of the mission are mainly derived from the mission objectives,

- The project budget is directly allocated to the acquisition of hardware components and software development. Therefore, the schedule and Coast Breakdown Structure can be directly derived from the Product Tree,

- In the case of students-driven projects, the personnel allocated to the project may change continuously and Business Agreement Structure can be neglected.

To take these specificities into account, we have based ourselves partially on the guidelines of the NASA system engineering manual [17], to adopt an MBSE Framework approach based on a model comprising a consistent set of views reflecting multiple viewpoints and stages in the nanosatellite project, as shown in Fig. 4:

As a reference framework for our work, we have partially used ESA's European Cooperation on Space Standardization (ECSS) standards [18] and NASA Systems Engineering Manual Guidelines [19], which provide free of charge the reference documents and tools necessary for mission management and system engineering.
The mission definition stage consists of 2 interdependent and highly iterative and recursive processes

The second step of functional decomposition, triggered by the validated Mission Requirements Review (MRR), is the process of identifying the "functions" that should be achieved at each level of the system to meet the validated NGOs.

Product breakdown structure (PBS): system decomposition into successive levels of hardware-oriented products or elements, articulated to perform the functions identified in the Functional Breakdown Process.

MASAT1 is a nanosatellite project initiated at the University of Sidi Mohamed Ben Abdellah, Fez, Morocco to put in place the basic and indispensable technologies (hardware and software) necessary to build a resilient, ready-to-fly CubeSat system, with efficient power management and low-cost mission control ground station [21]. The mission's main payload is an FPGA-based reconfigurable secondary onboard computer.
Based on the MCR document, the top-level mission requirements are set using the ECSS-E standard and the Mission Requirements Review (MRR) has been developed.
The Product Tree forms the basis for the project MBSE modeling approach adopted to create the product breakdown structure (PBS) and the work breakdown structure (WBS).

We take a simplified version of the process perspective, first modeling the context and requirements of the nanosatellite mission, and then modeling the structures and behaviors required to achieve those requirements. After that, parameters and analysis are then integrated into the system model to simulate the properties and workflow of the nanosatellite.

By integrating this methodology, as well as referring to the work of SSWG [6] [7] [8] and Guo et al. [10], we have organized our PBS model elements into packages structured by both SysML diagram type and hierarchy concurrently.

Following the same process, and in order to promote the use of the MASAT1 model as much as possible, all requirements were formulated according to the SRR document developed from the ECSS system engineering standards. Some subsystem requirements have been adjusted to meet the specific requirements of the MASAT1 project, such as the power subsystem design requirements, as shown in Fig. 14.
These tables describe the requirements and their relationship to other SysML design elements to facilitate requirements traceability, satisfaction, and verification.

The 'Verified By' column shows the specific test cases that determine how the system meets the requirement. For example, the "Bus System Activation" activity diagram (Fig. 23), which is part of the LEOP flow (Fig. 22), is used to verify operational requirement 100.1.6.
For example, Fig. 18 describes the power systems components, while Fig. 20 reveals the subsystem's internal connections and information flow.
Although MASAT1 mission uses passive attitude control, an attitude control mode has been included in ConOps to generalize the model proposed in this paper.

To improve communication, planning, management, and development, we implemented this approach, replacing ad hoc procedures in the work organization with process flow and model based on the different views of the system architecture.

The next step of this work is to improve the viability and practicality of the product breakdown structure model by integrating external analysis and simulation tools such as MATLAB and STK. The aim is to develop an executable SysML model with a graphical user interface to provide insight into how nanosatellites work.

This paper aims to build on the work of the cited article to provide a detailed, easy-to-understand, and effective Model-Based Systems Engineering for those wishing to launch a CubeSat project, including the initial phases of preparation, management, and analysis, tailored for university projects carried out by cohorts of students.
Choosing to use package diagrams at this level of abstract modeling helps stakeholders understand the structure of the model and helps modelers build the model in a more organized way.
